title: Constant right upper quadrant pain and vomiting after a rich dinner
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 41-year-old social worker in the ED with constant right upper quadrant pain since last night that radiates to the shoulder tip, with vomiting, fever and chills, and earlier milder episodes after rich meals. The candidate then interprets her observations, blood results (including a beta-hCG) and an upper abdominal ultrasound report, gives the diagnosis and differentials, outlines management in the ED, answers her fear that this is a tumour and safety-nets.
focus: Acute right upper quadrant pain in a woman of reproductive age: diagnosing acute cholecystitis, excluding the dangerous differentials and managing it in the ED
stem: You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital on a weekday afternoon. Gabby Russo, a 41-year-old social worker, has come in with abdominal pain. The triage nurse has taken her observations, put in an IV cannula and sent bloods. The nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Gabby and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, her blood results and an ultrasound report. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer Gabby's question (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Gabby Russo, a 41-year-old social worker. You lie very still on the trolley with your hand over your right upper tummy and a vomit bag beside you. You are flushed, distressed and a little shivery, and you answer in short sentences because of the pain. Give details only when you are asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "Please, this pain under my ribs is unbearable. I've been up all night with it."

The pain (give only when asked)

  • Site: under the right ribcage (you point to it).
  • Onset: it came on suddenly last night at about 8 pm, after dinner. If asked what you ate: "A big creamy pasta with garlic bread, and dessert. I love rich food."
  • Course: constant since it started. It has never gone away and has got steadily worse through the night and into this afternoon. It does not come and go in waves.
  • Radiation: "It goes up into the tip of my right shoulder."
  • Character (if asked): a deep, constant ache.
  • Relieving and aggravating: "Nothing helps." You took two Panadol and a Nurofen at about 7 this morning but vomited them straight back up. Pressing on it hurts.
  • Severity: "It's 10 out of 10 now. I can't do anything." You could not go to work today, and your husband stayed home with the children.
  • Previous episodes: "I sometimes get a similar pain under my right ribs after a rich meal, but it's never lasted this long." Over the past few months it has happened a few times; each one lasted an hour or two and went away by itself. You never saw anyone about them.

Other symptoms (only when asked about each)

  • Nausea since the pain began. You have vomited several times overnight and this morning, first food, now yellow-green fluid. No blood in it.
  • Since early this morning you have felt hot and then cold and shivery (chills). You have not taken your temperature. No uncontrollable shaking.
  • No appetite at all since last night.

Negatives (only if asked about each)

  • No yellowing of the skin or eyes, no itch, no dark urine, no pale stools.
  • No confusion (your husband says you have been yourself).
  • No pain in the middle of the upper tummy going through to the back. No heartburn or reflux, no black stools, no vomiting blood.
  • No diarrhoea. Your bowels opened normally yesterday and you are passing wind. Your husband ate the same dinner and is fine.
  • No chest pain, no breathlessness, no cough, no palpitations.
  • No pain or burning passing urine, no blood in the urine.
  • Periods: you take the pill every day and have not missed any. Your last period (on the pill) was about 2 weeks ago and was normal. No vaginal bleeding or discharge. You do not think you could be pregnant. No dizziness or fainting.
  • No weight loss (you have been trying to lose weight), no night sweats, no lumps.
  • Hepatitis risks: no injecting drugs, no tattoos, no blood transfusions, one partner (your husband). No recent overseas travel.

Background (only when asked)

  • Past history: two children, the second born by caesarean section. Otherwise well. No hospital admissions and no medical conditions. At your last check-up your GP suggested you lose some weight.
  • Medications: Panadol or Nurofen when you need them for period pain, tummy pains and headaches (a few times a month). The combined contraceptive pill (if asked the name: Levlen ED). A multivitamin. Nothing else.
  • Allergies: "Only hayfever." No allergies to any medicines.
  • Family history: your mother had a hysterectomy at 52 and her gallbladder taken out at 46, and she has high blood pressure. Your father has high blood pressure and had a heart attack 3 years ago; he is well after rehab. Your siblings are well.
  • Social: never smoked. A glass of red wine with dinner on weeknights and an extra one on weekends. You are a social worker and walk a fair bit at work. You cook at home and have takeaway on weekends, and you like rich food. You live with your husband and your 2 children. You are well supported.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: "I don't know what it is."
  • Concern: "These pains keep coming back. I'm scared it's a tumour." You are worried about your children.
  • Expectation: you want the pain to stop and to find out what this is.
  • Question to raise once in Part 1: "Could this be a tumour?" A good candidate acknowledges the worry and says they will know more once the tests are back, without false reassurance.

The nurse and how Gabby changes

  • If asked for observations, the nurse gives the triage set: RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 126/78, HR 110 regular, temperature 38.6 °C, alert, pain 10/10, BGL 6.0 mmol/L.
  • If the candidate orders oral analgesia, the nurse says: "She's vomiting, she won't keep tablets down."
  • If the candidate orders IV analgesia, the nurse gives it. About 10 minutes later Gabby says the pain is down to about 6/10 and she can talk more easily, but her right upper tummy is still very tender. Without it she stays at 10/10.
  • If the candidate orders an antiemetic, the nurse gives it and the vomiting settles.
  • Partway through, the nurse says: "She's just vomited a small amount of yellow-green fluid, and she's shivering."
  • If asked about a pregnancy test: "A serum beta-hCG went with the triage bloods. The result will come with the others."
  • If asked for blood cultures, the nurse takes them.
  • If asked for a bedside ECG: sinus tachycardia 110/min, normal axis, no ST or T wave changes.
  • If asked for a urine dipstick: negative for blood, leucocytes, nitrites and bilirubin.
  • If the candidate asks for blood results or imaging, the examiner says they will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: in severe pain and distressed, lying very still, flushed and slightly shivery. Alert and oriented. Height 168 cm, weight 92 kg (BMI about 33).
  • Hands, eyes and skin: warm peripheries, CRT 2 seconds. Sclerae not yellow, no jaundice. No stigmata of chronic liver disease. Mucous membranes dry.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended, moves with breathing. Healed Pfannenstiel (caesarean) scar. No visible mass.
  • Abdomen, palpation: marked tenderness in the right upper quadrant with voluntary guarding there. Murphy's sign positive (she catches her breath on deep inspiration when the gallbladder area is pressed); no catch when the same is done on the left. Mild epigastric tenderness, the rest of the abdomen soft. No rebound tenderness, no rigidity. No palpable gallbladder or mass. Liver and spleen not enlarged.
  • Percussion and auscultation: no percussion tenderness away from the right upper quadrant, no shifting dullness. Bowel sounds present and normal.
  • Renal angles: not tender. Hernial orifices: normal.
  • Chest: equal expansion, resonant, clear breath sounds including the right base. Heart: dual heart sounds, no murmurs.
  • Pelvic or rectal examination: if offered, the examiner says it is not needed.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms Gabby's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Acknowledges her 10/10 pain and vomiting with empathy and asks the nurse for IV (not oral) analgesia and an antiemetic early, without waiting until the end of the history.
check.d: Credit if the candidate switches to IV analgesia after the nurse points out she is vomiting.

check.x: Responds to her fear of a tumour by acknowledging it and saying the tests will help answer it, without false reassurance; uses plain language.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: under the right ribcage, radiating to the right shoulder tip
Onset and course: sudden at about 8 pm last night after a rich dinner, constant since and getting worse (not settling within hours)
Severity and impact: now 10/10, cannot do anything, off work
Modifying factors: nothing helps; painkillers vomited straight back up

check.x: Asks about associated symptoms and elicits nausea and repeated vomiting (food then bile, no blood), anorexia, and fever with chills since this morning.
check.d: The critical element is eliciting the fever and chills.

check.x: Elicits the previous shorter episodes of right upper quadrant pain after rich meals over the past few months.
Asks about biliary obstruction and cholangitis: jaundice, itch, dark urine, pale stools and confusion (all absent).
check.d: Score if at least 3 of the 5 are asked, including jaundice.

check.x: Asks about pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy: last period, contraception and chance of pregnancy, vaginal bleeding, faintness.
Screens for the other causes:

kids.x: Pancreatitis and peptic ulcer: epigastric pain through to the back, NSAID use (elicits occasional Nurofen, a few times a month), reflux, haematemesis or melaena
Gastroenteritis and obstruction: diarrhoea, others unwell after the same meal, bowels open and passing wind
Hepatitis and malignancy: hepatitis risk factors (injecting drugs, tattoos, transfusions, travel) and weight loss or night sweats
Extra-abdominal: chest pain, breathlessness or cough (ACS, right lower lobe pneumonia), urinary symptoms

check.x: Takes the past history, medications and allergies: caesarean section for her second child, GP advice to lose weight, Panadol and Nurofen when needed, the oral contraceptive pill, a multivitamin, hayfever only (no drug allergies).
Takes the family history and elicits her mother's gallbladder surgery at 46 (and her father's heart attack).

Takes the social history: never smoked, quantifies alcohol (a glass of wine on weeknights, an extra on weekends), diet rich in fatty food, social worker, lives with husband and 2 children, no overseas travel.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: she fears a tumour because the pains keep returning, worries about her children and wants the pain to stop.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs: notes she is in severe pain, lying still, flushed and shivery; asks for the full set of observations and identifies the fever (38.6 °C) and tachycardia (HR 110).
Checks the sclerae and skin for jaundice (none), looks for stigmata of chronic liver disease and assesses hydration (dry mucous membranes) and BMI.
Palpates the abdomen systematically, starting away from the pain, finds right upper quadrant tenderness with guarding and elicits a positive Murphy's sign.
check.d: Credit, but do not require, checking for the catch on the left side.

check.x: Looks for peritonitis and other causes: rebound or percussion tenderness, rigidity, bowel sounds, liver edge and a palpable gallbladder or mass, the caesarean scar, renal angles and hernial orifices.
check.d: Score if at least 4 are examined, including rebound or rigidity.

check.x: Auscultates the chest including the right base and the heart, and asks for a bedside ECG and urine dipstick.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: temperature 38.6 rising to 38.8 °C in the yellow zone and severe pain (yellow-zone additional criterion) calling for a clinical review; HR 110 to 114, BP and SpO2 in the white zone: febrile and unwell but not shocked.
Interprets the WCC of 15.8 with neutrophilia and the CRP of 142 as acute inflammation, consistent with cholecystitis.

Interprets the LFTs and lipase: normal bilirubin with only mildly raised ALP, GGT and ALT (under 1.5 times the upper limit), common in cholecystitis, so a duct stone or cholangitis is less likely; normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely.
States that the serum beta-hCG (below 2 IU/L) is negative, so she is not pregnant and ectopic pregnancy is excluded.

Interprets the ultrasound as acute calculous cholecystitis: distended gallbladder, wall 6 mm, pericholecystic fluid, stones with one impacted in the neck, sonographic Murphy's sign; CBD 4 mm and not dilated; no mass.

Gives acute calculous cholecystitis as the most likely diagnosis, justified by at least 4 of: constant RUQ pain for about 20 hours after a rich meal, shoulder tip radiation, earlier postprandial episodes, fever and vomiting, Murphy's sign, raised WCC and CRP, the ultrasound, and her risk factors (female, 41, BMI 33, parous, OCP, mother's cholecystectomy).
Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a feature for or against it from this case: ascending cholangitis, acute pancreatitis, perforated peptic ulcer, ectopic pregnancy, hepatitis.
check.d: Also credit biliary colic, appendicitis, right lower lobe pneumonia or ACS with a reason.

check.x: Management
Analgesia and supportive care: titrated IV opioid with an IV antiemetic, IV paracetamol, nil by mouth, IV crystalloid for dehydration.

Takes blood cultures, then starts IV antibiotics per eTG: amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4 to 7 mg/kg IV (adjusted body weight) as a single dose, interval by renal function, or ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily if gentamicin is contraindicated.
check.d: Credit any correct eTG regimen; the critical elements are cultures before antibiotics and an appropriate IV regimen. Her hayfever is not a drug allergy.

check.x: Refers to the general surgical team for admission and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission.
Plans VTE prophylaxis after risk assessment (obesity, the combined pill, surgery) and repeat LFTs, with duct imaging if they rise or jaundice develops.

Explains to Gabby in plain words that a gallstone has blocked and inflamed her gallbladder, that the scan showed no lump in the liver, gallbladder or pancreas, and that she needs to stay in hospital and will probably have her gallbladder removed; checks her understanding.
check.d: Credit telling her the removed gallbladder is checked under the microscope as routine.

check.x: Safety netting
Tells Gabby to call the nurse at once for at least 2 of: shaking chills, yellow skin or eyes, worse or spreading pain, feeling faint or confused.
Asks the nurse for at least hourly observations and to escalate a rising HR, falling BP, rising fever, new confusion or any red-zone value (rapid response).

part2.lead: Here are Gabby's observations, her blood results and the ultrasound report.
part2.patient:
Question 4 opens with Gabby's own question. React to the answer:

  • If told the scan showed gallstones and no lump, be relieved: "So it's not cancer? I've been so scared."
  • Then ask: "Will I need an operation? Who will look after the kids?" Accept it if the candidate explains kindly why she must stay (offering to call her husband helps).
  • If the candidate uses jargon (cholecystitis, laparoscopic, histology), ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Triage set at 15:20 and the nurse's repeat set at 16:20, both on room air.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: the 16:20 pain score is blank. If IV analgesia was ordered in Part 1, tell the candidate it is 6/10 after IV analgesia; otherwise tell them it is 10/10 and no analgesia has been given.
  • Read: at 15:20 the temperature of 38.6 °C is in the yellow zone and severe pain (10/10) meets the yellow-zone additional criteria; HR 110, BP 126/78, RR 18 and SpO2 97% on room air are white. At 16:20 the temperature is 38.8 °C (yellow) and HR 114 (white), BP 122/74; she is shivering and has vomited again.
  • Meaning: a persisting fever with tachycardia and chills is a systemic inflammatory response; she is not shocked and nothing is in the red zone.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review within 30 minutes (this review) and more frequent observations; take blood cultures, give analgesia, fluids and antibiotics; call a rapid response if any value enters the red zone.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: very severe RUQ pain, vomiting, febrile. IV cannula, bloods sent
Repeat set: shivering, vomited small amount of bile. Pain score: see examiner

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Gabby Russo. Collected 15:25 at cannulation. Sample not haemolysed. No previous results on file.
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 15.8 with neutrophils 13.1 and CRP 142: acute inflammation. Bilirubin 16 normal; ALP 124, GGT 48 and ALT 41 only mildly raised (all under 1.5 times the upper limit); AST, albumin and INR normal. Lipase 38 normal. Beta-hCG below 2. UEC normal; lactate 1.4 normal.
  • Meaning: inflammatory markers fit acute cholecystitis (WCC below 18 is in keeping with mild disease). Mild LFT changes are common from inflammation next to the liver; a normal bilirubin makes a common bile duct stone and cholangitis less likely, and these LFTs do not meet the TG18 acute cholangitis criterion for cholestasis (bilirubin ≥34 µmol/L or LFTs >1.5 × ULN). Normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely. She is not pregnant: ectopic excluded, and imaging, drugs and theatre are safe. Normal renal function allows gentamicin; normal lactate means no hypoperfusion.
  • Changes: supports IV antibiotics and surgical admission; repeat LFTs in 24 hours, and image the duct if they rise or she becomes jaundiced.

handover.label: Ultrasound of the upper abdomen
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the upper abdomen (liver, gallbladder, biliary tree, pancreas, right kidney), 17:05.

Clinical details: 41-year-old woman, constant right upper quadrant pain since 20:00 yesterday radiating to the right shoulder tip, vomiting, fever 38.8 °C, Murphy's sign positive. WCC 15.8, CRP 142, beta-hCG negative. ?Acute cholecystitis.

Findings:

  • Gallbladder: distended. Wall diffusely thickened to 6 mm and oedematous, with a small rim of pericholecystic fluid. Multiple mobile echogenic calculi up to 14 mm with posterior acoustic shadowing. A 12 mm calculus is impacted in the gallbladder neck and does not move with change in position. Positive sonographic Murphy's sign. No gas in the wall, no wall defect, no collection and no focal mass.
  • Bile ducts: common bile duct 4 mm, seen to the pancreatic head. No intrahepatic or extrahepatic duct dilatation. No duct calculus seen.
  • Liver: normal size, mildly increased echogenicity in keeping with mild steatosis. No focal lesion.
  • Pancreas: normal size and echotexture, no mass, no peripancreatic fluid.
  • Right kidney: normal size, no hydronephrosis or calculus.
  • Other: no free fluid. No right pleural effusion.

Conclusion: acute calculous cholecystitis with a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. Common bile duct not dilated; no duct stone seen. No focal liver, gallbladder or pancreatic mass. Mild hepatic steatosis.
handover.model:
• Read: distended gallbladder, wall 6 mm (4 mm or more is thickened), pericholecystic fluid, multiple stones with one impacted in the neck, positive sonographic Murphy's sign. No gas in the wall, perforation or collection. CBD 4 mm, no duct dilatation or duct stone. No mass. Mild fatty liver.
  • Meaning: confirms acute calculous cholecystitis from the impacted neck stone. A normal duct with a normal bilirubin makes choledocholithiasis and cholangitis unlikely. Normal pancreas fits the normal lipase. No mass seen, which answers much of her fear of a tumour. Under TG18 this is a definite diagnosis, mild (Grade I): no local complication, WCC below 18, under 72 hours, no organ dysfunction. The fatty liver fits her weight and explains part of the mild ALT rise.
  • Changes: admit under general surgery for IV antibiotics and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy this admission.

ask: You are now calling the general surgical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Gabby Russo, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Gabby now, here in the emergency department.
Gabby asks you, "Is this a tumour? What happens now?" Please answer her, including what she and the nurses should watch for.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; Gabby Russo, 41.
  • Situation: acute calculous cholecystitis; febrile, Murphy's positive; requesting surgical admission.
  • Background: constant RUQ pain since 20:00 yesterday after a rich dinner, radiating to the right shoulder tip, vomiting, fever and chills; earlier short postprandial episodes; BMI 33, combined OCP, occasional Nurofen, no drug allergies; mother had a cholecystectomy.
  • Assessment: T 38.6 to 38.8 °C (yellow zone), HR 114, BP normal, not shocked; WCC 15.8, CRP 142; bilirubin normal, ALP, GGT and ALT mildly raised; lipase normal; beta-hCG negative; ultrasound: wall 6 mm, pericholecystic fluid, impacted neck stone, CBD 4 mm, no mass.
  • Recommendation: I have started / am starting IV analgesia, fluids, blood cultures and IV antibiotics; please review for admission and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

Acute calculous cholecystitis: constant RUQ pain for about 20 hours after a rich meal, shoulder tip radiation, earlier postprandial episodes, fever, vomiting, Murphy's sign, raised WCC and CRP, ultrasound findings; risk factors (female, 41, BMI 33, parous, OCP, mother's cholecystectomy).

  • Ascending cholangitis: for: fever with chills, gallstones; against: no jaundice or confusion, bilirubin 16, CBD 4 mm.
  • Acute pancreatitis: for: gallstones, vomiting; against: lipase 38, no back pain, normal pancreas.
  • Perforated peptic ulcer: for: occasional NSAID (Nurofen a few times a month); against: pain and tenderness are maximal in the RUQ with only mild epigastric tenderness, no melaena or haematemesis, no rigidity, ultrasound explains the pain.
  • Ectopic pregnancy: against: OCP, normal period 2 weeks ago, beta-hCG negative.
  • Hepatitis: against: no jaundice or risk factors, ALT only 41.

1. Titrated IV opioid with an IV antiemetic, IV paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly; nil by mouth; IV crystalloid.
  2. Blood cultures, then IV antibiotics per eTG: amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4 to 7 mg/kg IV (adjusted body weight) single dose, interval by renal function; ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily if gentamicin contraindicated.
  3. General surgery: admit for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy this admission.
  4. VTE prophylaxis after risk assessment (obesity, OCP, surgery); repeat LFTs, duct imaging if they rise.

• Plain words: a gallstone has blocked and inflamed the gallbladder; the scan showed stones and no lump in the liver, gallbladder or pancreas; the gallbladder is checked under the microscope as routine.
  • What happens now: stay in hospital for a drip, antibiotics and pain relief, and keyhole removal of the gallbladder, probably this admission; checks understanding; offers to call her husband.
  • Call the nurse at once for shaking chills, yellow skin or eyes, worse or spreading pain, feeling faint.
  • Nurse: at least hourly observations; escalate rising HR, falling BP, rising fever, confusion or any red-zone value (rapid response).

ddx.for: Constant right upper quadrant pain for about 20 hours after a rich meal, radiating to the shoulder tip, with fever, chills, vomiting, earlier postprandial episodes, a positive Murphy's sign, WCC 15.8, CRP 142 and an ultrasound showing a 6 mm wall, pericholecystic fluid and an impacted neck stone.

ddx.dx: Ascending cholangitis from a common bile duct stone
ddx.for: Fever with chills, right upper quadrant pain, gallstones on ultrasound and mildly raised ALP and GGT.
ddx.against: No jaundice or confusion, bilirubin 16, common bile duct 4 mm with no duct stone, normal BP and lactate.

ddx.for: Gallstones on ultrasound, repeated vomiting, mild epigastric tenderness and wine most nights.
ddx.against: Lipase 38 is normal, the pain is in the right upper quadrant and goes to the shoulder, not through to the back, and the pancreas looks normal.

ddx.for: She takes Nurofen a few times a month and has severe constant pain with fever.
ddx.against: Pain maximal in the RUQ with only mild epigastric tenderness, no reflux or melaena, no rigidity or generalised peritonism, and the ultrasound shows a clear biliary cause.

ddx.for: A 41-year-old woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vomiting.
ddx.against: She takes the pill daily, had a normal period 2 weeks ago, has no bleeding or faintness, a normal BP and a serum beta-hCG below 2 IU/L.

ddx.for: Right upper quadrant pain with fever, a glass of wine most nights and a mildly raised ALT.
ddx.against: No jaundice, no hepatitis risk factors, ALT only 41 with a normal bilirubin, and the ultrasound explains the pain.

guide:
In Part 1, Gabby gives each part of the history only when asked. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The nurse reports the further vomit and shivering partway through. If the candidate orders oral analgesia, the nurse points out that she is vomiting. If the candidate asks for blood results or imaging in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over the observations, bloods and ultrasound report, then ask all four questions in order. The 16:20 pain score is blank: if IV analgesia was ordered in Part 1, give it as 6/10 after analgesia; otherwise give it as 10/10 with no analgesia given. Read out Gabby's question to open question 4. She asks her own follow-up questions while the candidate answers.

A high-performing candidate arranges IV analgesia and an antiemetic early. They characterise constant RUQ pain since last night with shoulder tip radiation, and elicit the fever and chills, the earlier postprandial episodes, the Nurofen use and her mother's gallbladder surgery. They screen for jaundice and cholangitis and ask about pregnancy. They elicit Murphy's sign and check for jaundice and peritonism, and examine the chest. In Part 2 they read the mild LFT changes with a normal bilirubin and duct as typical of cholecystitis, say the negative beta-hCG excludes ectopic pregnancy, and read the ultrasound as acute calculous cholecystitis. They give cultures, IV antibiotics and analgesia and refer for early cholecystectomy, and they answer the tumour question honestly and kindly.

A borderline candidate takes the pain history but misses the fever, pregnancy or jaundice questions or Murphy's sign, calls it biliary colic, or leaves out blood cultures or surgical referral. A failing candidate plans discharge with oral analgesia, or falsely reassures her ("it's definitely not cancer") before seeing any results.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute calculous cholecystitis

Gabby has had sudden, constant right upper quadrant pain for about 20 hours, starting after a rich dinner. It radiates to the right shoulder tip, which is pain referred through the phrenic nerve from irritation of the diaphragm. She has nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever with chills. The milder postprandial episodes over the past few months were probably biliary colic. This time the pain has not settled within a few hours, and she has fever and a positive Murphy's sign, so the cystic duct has stayed blocked and the gallbladder is inflamed.

She has the classic risk factors for cholesterol stones: female, around forty, a BMI over 30, parous, taking oestrogen (the combined pill), a rich, fatty diet, and a mother who had a cholecystectomy at 46.

Under the Tokyo Guidelines (TG18) she has a definite diagnosis: local signs (Murphy's sign, RUQ tenderness), systemic signs (fever, raised WCC and CRP) and confirming imaging. It is mild (Grade I): WCC below 18, no palpable mass, symptoms for under 72 hours, no local complication and no organ dysfunction.

What to expect on examination and investigation

  • Examination: in pain and lying still, febrile and tachycardic, RUQ tenderness with a positive Murphy's sign, and guarding (rigidity if the gallbladder has perforated).
  • Ultrasound: the first-line test for biliary disease. It shows gallstones, a distended gallbladder, a thickened wall (4 mm or more), pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy's sign. It also measures the common bile duct and looks for a mass.

Taking the history

Use reading time to list the causes of RUQ pain and let them guide the questions. Group the questions by symptom cluster: biliary (fever, jaundice), pancreatic (back pain, alcohol), peptic (NSAIDs, melaena), hepatic (risk factors), gynaecological (last period, pregnancy) and extra-abdominal (chest pain, cough). Ask how the pain affects her day. Biliary pain is not always in the RUQ: it can be epigastric or hard to localise. Back up each differential with the positives and negatives that are relevant to it.

Differentials that matter

  • Ascending cholangitis: a stone in the common bile duct can cause infection behind the blockage. Look for Charcot's triad (fever, RUQ pain, jaundice), and confusion and hypotension in Reynolds' pentad. It needs urgent ERCP decompression. A normal bilirubin and a non-dilated duct make it unlikely here.
  • Gallstone pancreatitis: a stone passing the ampulla can cause pancreatitis. This gives epigastric pain radiating to the back with a lipase more than 3 times the upper limit.
  • Perforated peptic ulcer: NSAID use is a risk factor. It typically causes sudden severe epigastric pain with generalised peritonism. If it is suspected, arrange an erect chest X-ray or CT.
  • Ectopic pregnancy: always check a beta-hCG in a woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, whatever her contraception.
  • Others: biliary colic, viral or alcohol-related hepatitis, appendicitis (a high-lying appendix), right lower lobe pneumonia and ACS (her father had a heart attack). These last two are why the chest is examined and an ECG is done.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: the temperature is in the yellow zone and severe pain is a yellow-zone additional criterion on the NSW chart, so she needs a clinical review and closer observations. She is tachycardic but not shocked.
  • Bloods: WCC and CRP are raised. Mildly abnormal LFTs are common in cholecystitis because of inflammation next to the liver. A normal bilirubin with ALP and GGT under 1.5 times the upper limit does not point to a duct stone: these LFTs do not meet the TG18 acute cholangitis criterion for cholestasis (bilirubin ≥34 µmol/L or LFTs >1.5 × ULN). If the bilirubin rises or jaundice develops, image the duct (MRCP) or arrange an intraoperative cholangiogram. A normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely, and the negative beta-hCG excludes pregnancy.
  • Ultrasound: confirms cholecystitis with an impacted neck stone. The duct is normal and there is no mass. The mild fatty liver fits her weight.

Management

  • Analgesia: titrated IV opioid with an IV antiemetic, plus IV paracetamol. She cannot keep tablets down.
  • Nil by mouth and IV crystalloid.
  • Blood cultures, then IV antibiotics as eTG recommends: amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4 to 7 mg/kg IV as a single dose (adjusted body weight in obesity), with the interval set by renal function and empirical gentamicin for no more than 72 hours. If gentamicin is contraindicated, give ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily.
  • Admission under general surgery for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission. Delaying the operation risks recurrence and complications.
  • VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis (obesity, combined pill, surgery). Review her contraception after surgery.
  • If she deteriorates (sepsis, peritonitis, jaundice), escalate to senior surgical review and consider gangrene, perforation or cholangitis.

Answering "Is it a tumour?"

Answer honestly and kindly. The scan shows gallstones and an inflamed gallbladder, which explains her symptoms, and there is no lump in the liver, gallbladder or pancreas. The removed gallbladder is routinely examined under the microscope. Do not offer reassurance before the results are back.

Safety netting

In hospital, Gabby and the nurses report shaking chills, yellow skin or eyes, worsening or spreading pain, faintness or confusion at once. These can mean cholangitis, perforation or sepsis. Any red-zone observation triggers a rapid response. After the operation she sees her GP in 1 to 2 weeks for the wound, the histology, and support with weight and diet. She returns to the ED for fever, jaundice, worsening pain or a red, discharging wound.
points: Biliary colic settles within a few hours. Constant RUQ pain lasting longer, with fever, Murphy's sign and raised WCC and CRP, is acute cholecystitis.
Gallstone risk factors: female, around forty, obesity, parity, oestrogen (OCP), fatty diet and a family history of gallbladder disease.
Always check a beta-hCG in a woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, and consider extra-abdominal causes such as right lower lobe pneumonia and ACS.
Mild LFT changes are common in cholecystitis. A raised bilirubin, jaundice or a dilated duct suggests a duct stone, and with fever, cholangitis, which needs urgent decompression.
Ultrasound is the first test: gallstones, a wall of 4 mm or more, distension, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy's sign.
Management is IV analgesia and an antiemetic, fluids, blood cultures, IV antibiotics as eTG recommends, and admission for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
